source.title: Articulation Upper Bounds for Language Models
source.authors: Alexander Spangher; Daniel E. Ho; Diyi Yang; Noah Goodman; Sanmi Koyejo

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses observational scaling-law analysis as a framework for studying how concept-transmission recovery changes with model capability. It does not test the claim’s language-model pretraining-loss laws or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The study measures transmission recovery and capability-index scaling, not held-out cross-entropy loss, parameter/token/compute scaling of loss, or a compute-optimal allocation. Its recovery-scaling results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version. Prompt-optimization benchmark results are about the study’s own method and do not measure the claim’s object.
record.test_reason: The study borrows observational scaling laws (Ruan et al.) as a framework. It fits a novel transmission measure against a capability index z, which is logit AUC on the authors' own 240-item battery. That measure is reliability-corrected agreement with a leave-one-out panel consensus. The study measures no pretraining loss and no parameter, token or compute scaling of loss. It does not test compute-optimal allocation or shape effects. The closest candidate is V6. However, its x-axis is a capability score rather than scale or pretraining loss, and its y-axis is agreement with other models rather than task performance against ground truth. Its results are therefore a related construct, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly right but incomplete. The authors conclude that most of 1,270 concepts transmit now (321) or are projected to with scale (884). They find 65 bounded concepts tied to identity and social-group awareness that larger models, more labels and examples do not lift. They hold that these limits are executor-relative, since humans agree moderately-to-highly on 76% of the bounded concepts with published studies. Their robustness appendix concedes that individual regime membership and the bounded count depend on the capability axis.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits observational recovery-versus-capability curves, using linear and logistic fits selected by AICc. It does not measure pretraining cross-entropy scaling or fit a parameter/token/compute-optimal loss law.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery-regime results vary with the capability axis: the bounded count is 65 on the paper’s z axis, 12 on the battery’s first component, and 273 on equally spaced ranks. Curve form, executor inclusion and thresholds also affect regime assignments; dropping the highest-z executor changes 12% of verdicts, especially reaches-to-rising assignments.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 1,270 concept curves of consensus agreement versus capability index z, 884 are rising, 321 reach a ceiling and 65 are bounded (77 excluded as noisy). Refitting without the top executor predicts it with median error .062. Regime counts depend strongly on the capability axis: bounded is 65 on z, 12 on the first principal component, and 273 on equally spaced ranks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Observational scaling of inter-model concept transmission against a capability index is regular enough to forecast the next executor. Its plateau classification depends on axis construction.

fits_no_version.finding: Planted code-checkable rules are recovered at AUC .51 by a 1B receiver, .61 at 3B, .73 at 8B and about .80 from 14B. An executor far beyond the panel (GPT-5.6, z=4.78) leaves 0 of 65 bounded concepts above the planted reference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recovery of simple planted rules rises smoothly with receiver size, while some socially anchored concepts plateau even past the panel. This is a possible limit on downstream predictability, but it is measured as agreement with the panel consensus.

record.problems: The measured outcome is a novel reconstruction-based transmission-recovery measure, not language-model cross-entropy loss. Recovery-regime membership is uncertain for individual criteria: 163 of 1,270 have less than a .6 chance of retaining their printed regime under resampling. Regime counts and contrasts change under alternative capability axes; the paper also reports that the rising cutoff has no external criterion validating it. The recovery measure’s validation is uneven across levels, and the authors state there is no validation evidence across regimes.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were included for the supervised prompt-optimization benchmark comparisons because those report the study’s method performance, not language-model loss or the claim’s predicted behavior. Literature statistics cited in the paper were not entered as study results.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; not measured.
Extrapolation of loss from small to large runs. The held-out-executor prediction (median error .062) concerns the agreement measure on a capability axis, not loss.
Depth, width and architecture at fixed parameter count; not studied.
Other modalities or training regimes; not studied.
Downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss. The study uses a capability index and a consensus-agreement measure instead.
Fit-dependence of loss exponents or the compute-optimal split. The axis and fit sensitivity reported (R9, R10) concern regime classification of the agreement measure.

missing.what: Planted-rule AUC by receiver parameter size (.51 at 1B to about .80 at 14B), the only result plotted against model size rather than z
Frontier executor extension: GPT-5.6 y on bounded, control and planted strata versus the panel's top three

record.verdict_notes: This is a borderline call against a V6/T3 reading. The study uses 'scaling laws' in the observational sense, with a self-built capability battery as the x-axis and inter-model consensus agreement as the y-axis, so it does not measure downstream performance versus scale or loss. The supervised prompt-optimization results are the authors' own method and are correctly left out. R3 (logistic .051) and R4 (line .075) match Table 9.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger runs’ held-out pretraining loss from smaller runs; the study predicts recovery for a different measure.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and architecture details on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream-task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss; the study measures concept-transmission recovery instead.

Dependence of loss-scaling exponents and compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, and departures of loss curves from a power law. The study reports fit and axis sensitivity for recovery scaling, not loss scaling or compute-optimal allocation.

rows.check: The regime counts are classification outcomes of the authors' own decision rule (AICc, planted reference, slope cutoff .35). They are not a scaling measurement of any claim version. The values are correct as extracted.
